# Count Week

Every year on the Saturday before Christmas, Walter Pruitt counted birds in a circle fifteen miles across, and every year he got the worst part of it: the sewage lagoons, the Methodist cemetery, and a quarter mile of frozen ditch behind the Tractor Supply.

He didn't mind. Thirty-eight years ago he'd asked for it, because the lagoons never froze all the way over, and where there's open water in December there are ducks, and where there are ducks there are sometimes surprises. Ruth used to say he had a talent for loving the places nobody else wanted. She meant it as a compliment, mostly. She'd said it about herself, too, the first year they were married, when he took her to the lagoons on a date and she stood in the smell with her hands in her coat pockets and laughed until she had to sit down on the hood of the car.

This was the first year he did the count without her.

He arrived at 7:10, before full light, and sat in the truck with the heater running and his clipboard on his knee. The tally sheet was the same one they'd always used, printed from the regional compiler's email, species listed in taxonomic order. Canada Goose. Mallard. American Black Duck. Ruth had kept the sheet; Walter had kept the binoculars. She had the better handwriting and he had the better eyes, and between the two of them they were one competent birder. That was the joke. They'd told it at the compilation dinner for three decades, and people had laughed politely at it for most of them.

He got out. The cold went straight through his jeans.

The lagoons gave him what they usually gave him. Forty-one Mallards. A dozen Buffleheads, bobbing and diving like wind-up toys. Six Ring-necked Ducks. A single Pied-billed Grebe, which he was glad to see, because some years there wasn't one and the absence felt personal. He wrote the numbers down in his own cramped hand, which slanted badly and which Ruth had once described as "a man falling down stairs."

By nine he'd moved to the cemetery. It sat on a rise above the river, and the old cedars along its northern edge held robins in winter, and juncos, and in a good year a Hermit Thrush skulking low in the hedge. Ruth was not buried here. Ruth was buried forty miles away, next to her parents, which had been her wish and which he had honored. But he found that he walked the rows more slowly than usual anyway, reading names he'd read a hundred times.

He was standing by the Hollenbeck family obelisk when the bird landed.

It dropped out of a cedar onto the frozen grass maybe thirty feet from him, and for a second his brain simply refused it. It was robin-shaped but wrong. Slate-gray back. Throat and eyebrow a deep, burning orange, like a coal someone had blown on. A dark band across the chest, clean as a necklace. Orange bars on the wings.

He knew what it was. He had known what it was since he was nine years old, paging through his grandfather's Peterson guide, when he'd stopped on that plate and thought it was the most beautiful bird in the book and also the one he would never see, because it lived in the dark wet forests of Oregon and Washington, two thousand miles from here.

Varied Thrush.

It hopped twice. It flipped a leaf with its bill. It looked at him, or seemed to, with one black eye.

Walter did not move. He did not raise his binoculars, because he was afraid the motion would flush it, and because he didn't need them. He just stood there in the cold among the Hollenbecks and the Garveys and the infant Mary Louise Strand, 1911–1912, and looked.

Later he would think about how long it lasted. Forty seconds? A minute? It felt longer, the way certain moments in a marriage feel longer, the way a hospital night does, or a first kiss. Then a truck downshifted out on Route 9 and the thrush was gone, up and over the cedars and down toward the river, and Walter was an old man standing alone in a cemetery with his mouth open.

He knew what would happen next. He'd seen it happen to other people.

A Varied Thrush in this county would be a first record, or close to it. The compiler would want documentation. A photograph, ideally. At minimum, a detailed written description and a second observer. The records committee would review it. They would be polite. They would ask whether he'd considered an aberrant robin. They would note, gently, his age, and the lack of corroboration, and maybe, if they'd heard, his recent loss. And the sighting would go into the database with an asterisk, or it would not go in at all.

Ruth had carried the camera. Ruth would have gotten the photo; she was fast, she was always fast. And if she hadn't, she'd have been his second observer, and her word had always been worth more than his in rooms full of people, because she was calm and precise and did not get excited about things.

He stood there a long time.

Then he walked back to the truck, got in, and turned the heater up. He took out the clipboard. He found the thrushes on the tally sheet — Eastern Bluebird, Hermit Thrush, American Robin — and he wrote *robins, 23*, which was true, and *Hermit Thrush, 1*, which was also true, from the hedge on the way out.

He looked at the blank margin for a while.

At the compilation dinner that night, over chili in the basement of the Lutheran church, people would go around the table and report their highlights, and someone would ask about the lagoons, and he would say the grebe was back. And they'd say good, good. And somebody who knew would squeeze his shoulder.

He didn't write it down. Not because they wouldn't believe him. Because for thirty-eight years, everything he'd seen, he'd seen with someone, and every bird had belonged to both of them, and every count had been a thing they made together, and now here was one sighting, the most beautiful one of his life, that belonged only to him.

He thought she would have understood that. He thought she would have laughed.

He put the truck in gear and drove to the Tractor Supply, where the ditch was frozen solid and there was, as usual, nothing at all.
